pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that can cluster on the tender tips and flower buds, leaving sticky honeydew. Borage is otherwise seldom bothered by pests, and its flowers pull in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids, so light infestations often clear on their own. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles the rest. Some gardeners even let borage collect aphids as a decoy to keep them off nearby crops.
pests.note_seasoned: Borage is generally untroubled by insect pests; extension descriptions note it is not usually bothered and has no significant pest problems. When aphids do appear they colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew, but the nectar-rich flowers recruit the aphid predators (ladybugs, hoverflies, lacewings) that keep them in check. Borage is sometimes grown deliberately as an insectary or banker planting for this reason. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on the leaves, most common in warm, humid, still, or crowded conditions and without enough air movement. It is borage's main disease. Give plants plenty of room, grow them in full sun, water the soil rather than the leaves, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Borage's signature disease, and essentially its only regular one; it develops in warm, humid, still, and crowded plantings, and worsens as summer heat and humidity build (which is why borage is grown in the cool season in hot climates). Manage culturally with full sun, generous spacing for airflow, base watering, and removal of affected foliage rather than by spraying.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot in wet soil
diseases.note_beginner: Borage is drought-tolerant and hates soggy soil. Cold, wet, poorly drained ground can rot its roots and stem base, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line. Plant in well-drained soil and do not overwater.
diseases.note_seasoned: Borage tolerates dry soil and is intolerant of waterlogging, so the standing failure is root and crown rot (and seedling damping-off) in cold, wet, poorly drained ground. It is a prevention story, not a treatment one: site in well-drained soil, water only when the soil dries, and avoid heavy, water-retentive beds. This is the drought-tolerant plant's usual wet-soil caveat rather than a disease borage is specifically prone to.
